extracted.intended_audience: educated early-18th-century readers of The Spectator — theatre-goers, readers of poetry, parents and educators interested in taste and manners
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical-essay guidance on literary taste, theatrical practice, public morals, and education (notably travel as part of schooling). The page mixes literary criticism (Milton, drama), theatrical/naturalistic staging commentary, public-health/legal suggestions about wine vending, and practical advice about travel and manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cat-call as a theatrical instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cat-call is treated as an English musical instrument peculiar to the British stage; it 'very much Improves the Sound of Nonsense' and often accompanies the actor as a violin accompanies recitative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the cat-call to enhance and emphasize stage nonsense and to accompany an actor's delivery; it can replace an ancient chorus. The writer notes national development and 'great Improvements' in the instrument's playing (quavers and graces). Anti-pattern: using the cat-call outside its dramatic purpose (e.g., as a serenade by an angry lover) is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiated cat-call sounds to signal dramatic critique
rubrics_metrics.description: A practiced artist can play base and treble cat-calls (base for Tragedy, treble for Comedy), and has specific squeaks and sounds to denote dramatic faults (e.g., violation of the unities) or to aim at the poet vs. the player.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ distinct cat-call tones to match genre and to communicate critical judgments to the audience; composers/players may invent 'Smut-note, Fustian-note, Stupid-note' and an Act-tune to mark incorrigible plays. This treats audience vocalization as an encoded critical language rather than mere noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect and ensure purity of provisions (wine) for public health
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who import and ensure genuine wine (named example: Brooke and Hillier) deserve public gratitude for preventing adulteration that endangers health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic duty: officers should inspect itinerant vendors and carts to discover sources of provisions; vendors who mix wines knowing they are unsafe should be exposed and punished. Suggested institutional measures: oaths for wine venders, public reporting at quarter sessions, and severe legal liability (the letter even argues for treating deliberate adulteration that causes death as wilful murder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity and legal severity against adulteration
rubrics_metrics.description: False-selling of one liquor as another (e.g., mixing Herefordshire into Port) should not be excused as chance or manslaughter; intent to deceive makes the act culpable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend public presentment of offenders, jury instruction to investigate such delinquents, and strong punitive measures to deter those who 'play with Men's Lives' by preparing potentially noxious mixtures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel as the last step of education
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel should be 'really the last Step to be taken in the Institution of Youth' — beginning education with travel is backwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young persons should first acquire solid foundations (manners, basic learning, language, rules of behaviour). Sending youth abroad too early (with inadequate preparation) yields little benefit and may 'cause such a Dizziness in young empty Heads' that lasts a lifetime. Anti-pattern: sending lads away crying and snivelling under poor tutors, or treating travel as primary instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims of beneficial travel — customs, policies, and manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The true ends of visiting foreign parts are to observe foreign customs and politics, compare them to our own, unlearn awkward local peculiarities, and improve manners through wider, mixed conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travellers should use travel to see in what particulars other nations excel or fall short, and to correct local affectations. Travel is valuable when used to form judgment about institutions and behaviour, not merely to gape at sights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel to improve taste in antiquity and moral imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing the places described by ancient authors helps form taste and moral imagination by comparing text to original and by contemplating ruins to draw lessons on the uncertainty of human things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To profit, a traveller should be 'rightly turned' for such study and prepared (knowing the ancient languages reasonably well). Visiting the spots associated with great men may inspire emulation of their virtues — travel should be used to warm a 'generous Mind' toward virtuous examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properly prepared, guided travel (need for competent tutors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Young travellers sent with incompetent or ill-paid tutors gain little; being 'banished' with a poor scholar leads to staring and gaping rather than improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange travel with skilled masters who will prepare the traveller to observe and draw conclusions; do not substitute travel for the prior work of instruction. Anti-pattern: shipping a lad abroad under a cheap, incapable tutor and expecting education by exposure alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of epic action — include the expulsion to complete the Fall
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's representation of Adam and Eve's expulsion from Paradise completes the action of the Fall; without this the Fall-of-Man action would be incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An epic treating a moral or theological fall should represent the consequence and completion of that fall (here, the expulsion) to render the action whole and the drama complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of character portrayal and diction to rank and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton 'suits his Parts to the Actors whom he introduces' — e.g., Michael's person, port, and behaviour are appropriate to a high-ranking spirit, different from Raphael's sociable manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match language, behaviour, and descriptive detail to a character's rank and function; high characters should be represented in a manner 'suitable to a Spirit of the highest Rank'. This fitting enhances verisimilitude and moral effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scriptural and poetical materials with apt allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton weaves poetical parts of Scripture and allegory into his narration (e.g., prayers ascending like incense) to enrich meaning and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate venerable or sacred images and allegory where they naturally amplify the theme; such borrowings should feel proper and enhance the reader's understanding rather than appearing forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and contrast in incident and vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Delight in poetry arises from a contrast and opposition of incidents (e.g., moving from visions of sickness and death to scenes of mirth, love, jollity), and Milton's variety in his visions is praised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ contrasts (terror vs. mirth; horror of war vs. triumphs and festivals) to sustain interest and to move the reader through varied emotions. A sustained monotone in incident weakens effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid redundant, puerile, or ill-suited imagery in grand catastrophes
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton is commended for avoiding the 'redundant or puerile' inventions (like Ovid's wolves swimming among sheep) in descriptions of great catastrophes such as the Deluge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing great or solemn events, choose imagery that is dignified and apt to the magnitude of the subject; avoid idle or superfluous embellishments that diminish solemnity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of appropriate musical/musical-symbolic choices for occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: Martial drums at the break of a wedding morning are improper and offensive; softer airs better suit the occasion's sentimental tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select music (or musical symbolism) congruent with the moral/ceremonial purpose: weddings call for soft airs, not warlike sounds which suggest discord and brevity of joys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic mirth should be tempered with moral severity
rubrics_metrics.description: A reader who keeps 'Reason and Authority over all their Actions' prefers entertainments where mirth is 'seasoned with a certain Severity' — comedy should retain some moral seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In comedic entertainment, balance humour with moral or critical restraint so the laughter does not promote imitation of vice. Praises are given to performers (Mrs. Porter) who display honourable sentiments within comic or tragic roles.
